commands.name: kubectl
commands.summary: Command-line tool for controlling Kubernetes clusters.
commands.risk_reason: Deleting resources or applying bad configs can disrupt production workloads.
cautions: Confirm context and namespace first: kubectl config current-context.
`kubectl delete` has no undo — export objects and use --dry-run=server first.
Prefer declarative `apply -f` from Git over ad-hoc edit/patch, which causes drift.
commands.explanation: kubectl communicates with the Kubernetes API server to manage cluster resources. Always verify your current context with `kubectl config current-context` before running destructive commands in production.

flags.desc: Output format: wide, yaml, json, jsonpath
Preview what would happen without applying

examples.desc: List all production pods with node and IP info
Perform a rolling restart of the frontend deployment

commands.pro_tip: Set `kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=production` to avoid typing -n production on every command.

commands.name: kubectl get
commands.summary: List Kubernetes resources with flexible output options.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only unless combined with write operations.
commands.explanation: kubectl get is the primary read command for K8s. It lists resources with status. Output formats range from human-friendly tables to machine-parseable JSON/YAML. The -w flag watches for changes. Mastering -o and --field-selector transforms kubectl from a query tool into an automation backbone.

flags.desc: Format: json, yaml, wide, jsonpath, custom-columns

examples.desc: All pods across namespaces with node info

commands.pro_tip: Use `kubectl get pods -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.status.phase!="Running") | .metadata.name'` to programmatically find non-running pods — far more reliable than parsing tabular output.

commands.name: kubectl describe
commands.summary: Show detailed state and events for a Kubernetes resource.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: kubectl describe provides human-readable detail about any K8s resource: events, conditions, container specs, volume mounts, and more. The Events section at the bottom is the first place to look when a pod won't start — it shows exactly what Kubernetes tried and what failed.

examples.desc: Node capacity, allocatable resources, and conditions
Deployment strategy, rollout status, and events

commands.pro_tip: When a pod is stuck in Pending/CrashLoopBackOff, always check `kubectl describe pod` first — the Events section usually tells you exactly why (image pull error, insufficient resources, PVC not bound).

commands.name: kubectl logs
commands.summary: Fetch logs from containers in Kubernetes pods.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only log access.
commands.explanation: kubectl logs streams container logs from pods. The -c flag targets a specific container in multi-container pods. --previous shows logs from the last terminated container — essential for debugging crashes. -f follows live.

flags.desc: Print logs from previously terminated container
Lines of recent log to show
Stream logs from all pods matching label

examples.desc: Logs from the crashed previous container
Last 50 lines from all nginx pods

commands.pro_tip: Use `kubectl logs --previous` immediately when a pod restarts — the current container starts fresh, and crash logs disappear if you wait too long (especially with short log rotation).

commands.name: kubectl exec
commands.summary: Execute commands inside a running Kubernetes container.
commands.risk_reason: Direct container access; avoid in production when possible.
cautions: Changes made inside the container vanish on restart and are not tracked.
In production prefer logs, metrics and `kubectl debug` with an ephemeral container.
Commands run with the container’s privileges — a root shell can modify mounted volumes.
commands.explanation: kubectl exec runs commands inside a running container, similar to docker exec. The -- separator is required before the command. Use for live debugging — testing DNS resolution, checking env vars, verifying file contents — without redeploying.

examples.cmd: kubectl exec mypod -- env | grep DB

examples.desc: Test service connectivity from inside cluster

commands.pro_tip: Use `kubectl exec pod -- curl http://service.namespace.svc.cluster.local` to test service DNS and connectivity from within the cluster network — the most reliable way to verify network policies.

commands.name: kubectl apply
commands.summary: Apply a Kubernetes manifest to create or update resources.
commands.risk_reason: Modifies live cluster state; validate manifests before applying.
cautions: Applies immediately — run `kubectl diff -f` first.
A manifest with the wrong namespace or an old image tag can roll production back.
--prune and --force can delete or recreate objects.
commands.explanation: kubectl apply declaratively applies resource manifests from files or directories. It creates resources if they don't exist, and updates them if they do — using server-side merge. Always dry-run first in production with --dry-run=server.

flags.desc: client or server — preview without applying
Force apply by deleting and recreating

examples.desc: Apply all manifests in a directory

safer.why: Validate against the API server and admission webhooks.

commands.pro_tip: Always use `--dry-run=server` not `--dry-run=client` — server-side dry run runs full validation including admission webhooks, catching errors that client-side validation misses.

commands.name: kubectl rollout
commands.summary: Manage and monitor Kubernetes deployment rollouts.
commands.risk_reason: Rollback can revert production to a previous state.
cautions: `rollout undo` reverts to the previous ReplicaSet, which might not be the version you expect — check `rollout history` first.
`rollout restart` replaces every pod; make sure readiness probes and PodDisruptionBudgets are in place.
A forgotten `rollout pause` leaves the workload half-updated.
commands.explanation: kubectl rollout manages deployment rollouts: checking status, viewing history, pausing, resuming, and rolling back. Essential for zero-downtime deployments and incident response — a bad deploy can be reverted in seconds with rollout undo.
commands.pro_tip: Run `kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp --timeout=5m` in CI/CD pipelines — it blocks until the rollout completes (or fails), making the pipeline accurately reflect deploy success.

commands.name: helm
commands.summary: Kubernetes package manager: install, upgrade, and manage chart releases.
commands.risk_reason: Manages production workloads; test with --dry-run first.
cautions: Use `--dry-run --debug` or `helm diff upgrade` before upgrade/install.
`helm uninstall` deletes all release resources.
Pin chart versions (--version) so upgrades are reproducible.
commands.explanation: Helm manages Kubernetes applications as charts — versioned packages of manifests with configurable values. It handles install, upgrade, rollback, and uninstall with release tracking. The --dry-run flag and diff plugin are essential for safe production operations.

examples.desc: Show currently applied values for a release

commands.pro_tip: Install the helm-diff plugin (`helm plugin install https://github.com/databus23/helm-diff`) and use `helm diff upgrade` before every upgrade — shows exactly what will change in the cluster.

commands.name: kubectl top
commands.summary: Show CPU and memory resource usage for nodes and pods.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only; requires metrics-server installed.
commands.explanation: kubectl top shows real-time CPU and memory usage for nodes and pods, powered by the metrics-server addon. Unlike kubectl get (which shows requests/limits), top shows actual consumption. Essential for identifying resource-hungry pods and right-sizing requests.

examples.desc: Most memory-hungry pods across all namespaces
Live top CPU consumers across cluster

commands.pro_tip: Use `kubectl top pods --sort-by=memory` before scaling — it often reveals one rogue pod consuming 10x expected memory, letting you target the fix rather than scaling everything.

commands.name: kubectl debug
commands.summary: Debug pods and nodes by attaching ephemeral containers.
commands.risk_reason: Adds temporary containers to live pods.
commands.explanation: kubectl debug creates ephemeral debug containers in running pods (K8s 1.23+), copies pods with different images, or attaches a shell to a node. The solution to debugging distroless/scratch images that have no shell or tools.

flags.desc: Create a debug copy of the pod
Target container to share process namespace with

examples.desc: Add busybox debug container sharing target's process namespace
Debug a cluster node with ubuntu container
Create a debuggable copy of a pod

commands.pro_tip: Use `kubectl debug` with `--image=nicolaka/netshoot` — the netshoot image has tcpdump, curl, dig, ss, and 50+ network tools pre-installed, perfect for K8s network debugging.

commands.name: helm diff
commands.summary: Preview Helm upgrade changes before applying with helm-diff plugin.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only diff preview.
commands.explanation: The helm-diff plugin (install separately) shows a diff of what `helm upgrade` would change in the cluster — like `terraform plan` for Helm. Shows which Kubernetes resources will be added, modified, or deleted, and the exact field changes.

examples.desc: Show 5 lines of context around changes
Diff between two specific release revisions

commands.pro_tip: Make `helm diff upgrade` a mandatory step in your CI/CD review process — anyone approving a Helm upgrade should see the diff, not just the values file change.

commands.name: kubeconfig
commands.summary: Manage Kubernetes contexts and clusters in kubeconfig.
commands.risk_reason: Switching context applies all commands to a different cluster.
cautions: The active context decides which cluster receives your next command — the classic way to hit production by mistake.
Kubeconfig files contain credentials: keep permissions 600 and never commit them.
`kubectl config use-context` is persistent; prefer --context per command for risky operations.
commands.explanation: kubectl uses kubeconfig (~/.kube/config) to store cluster credentials and contexts. A context pairs a cluster with credentials and a namespace. Managing multiple clusters requires switching contexts — and verifying you're in the right one before destructive operations.

examples.desc: Set default namespace for current context

commands.pro_tip: Install kubectx and kubens (`brew install kubectx`) for fast context/namespace switching. Set a PS1 prompt that shows current context — catching wrong-cluster mistakes before they happen.

commands.name: crictl
commands.summary: CLI for CRI-compatible container runtimes (containerd, CRI-O).
commands.risk_reason: Low-level runtime access; bypasses Kubernetes scheduling.
cautions: Bypasses the Kubernetes API — removing containers/pods with crictl leaves the kubelet and API server inconsistent.
Usually requires root on the node; mistakes affect every pod on that node.
commands.explanation: crictl is the kubectl-equivalent for the Container Runtime Interface layer — directly managing containers and images in containerd or CRI-O without going through Kubernetes. Essential on K8s nodes when kubelet is broken or for low-level debugging.

examples.desc: List running containers on the node
Get logs from a container by runtime ID
Detailed container info at runtime level
Shell into container via runtime directly

commands.pro_tip: Use crictl when kubelet is down or a pod won't schedule but the container exists — `crictl ps -a` shows all containers at the runtime level regardless of Kubernetes state.

commands.name: flux
commands.summary: GitOps tool for continuous delivery to Kubernetes from Git.
commands.risk_reason: Automates cluster changes; misconfigured sources apply incorrect state.
cautions: Reconciliation applies whatever is in Git — a bad commit rolls out automatically.
`flux suspend/resume/delete` change how production is reconciled; check `flux get all -A` first.
Bootstrap writes to your Git repository and cluster — double-check the target repo and branch.
commands.explanation: Flux implements GitOps for Kubernetes — it continuously reconciles cluster state with Git repositories. Any manifests committed to the configured repo are automatically applied to the cluster. The flux CLI manages sources, kustomizations, helm releases, and reconciliation.

examples.desc: Show status of all flux resources
List all Helm releases managed by Flux

commands.pro_tip: Use `flux reconcile source git flux-system` before `flux reconcile kustomization` — forces a fresh git pull first, so you're reconciling against the latest committed state.

commands.name: argocd
commands.summary: GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes.
commands.risk_reason: Syncing applications applies cluster changes immediately.
cautions: `argocd app sync` applies changes immediately (and --prune deletes resources not in Git).
Check `argocd app diff <app>` first.
Auto-sync with self-heal reverts manual cluster changes.
commands.explanation: ArgoCD is a declarative GitOps CD tool for Kubernetes. It monitors Git repositories and ensures cluster state matches. The CLI manages applications, syncs state, and rolls back. Applications show as Synced/OutOfSync and Healthy/Degraded.

examples.desc: List all applications and their sync status
Trigger immediate sync for an application
Show diff between live state and desired state
Roll back to a specific revision

commands.pro_tip: Use `argocd app diff` before every manual sync in production — it shows the exact Kubernetes resource changes, equivalent to `terraform plan` for your GitOps workflow.

commands.name: velero
commands.summary: Backup, restore, and migrate Kubernetes cluster resources and persistent volumes.
commands.risk_reason: Restores overwrite existing resources; test in non-production first.
cautions: `velero restore` can overwrite existing resources and PVC data.
Check `velero backup describe` / `logs` and restore into a test namespace first.
Backups do not include volume data unless snapshots or file-system backup are configured.
commands.explanation: Velero backs up Kubernetes cluster state and persistent volume data to object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob). Enables disaster recovery, cluster migration, and namespace-level restore. Backups include all K8s objects and optionally PV snapshots.

examples.desc: List all backups and their status

commands.pro_tip: Always test restores, not just backups. Schedule a monthly `velero restore create --from-backup latest --include-namespaces test` in a non-prod cluster to verify backup integrity.

commands.name: kubectl delete
commands.risk_reason: Removes objects immediately; PVC/namespace deletion removes data.
cautions: Check context + namespace first: kubectl config current-context.
`delete ns` removes every resource inside — including PVCs and data.
--all and label selectors can match more than you expect — run `kubectl get` with the same selector first.
--force --grace-period=0 skips cleanup and can corrupt stateful workloads.
commands.explanation: Deletes resources by name, label, file or --all.

flags.caution: Deletes every object in the namespace.

commands.name: kubectl scale
commands.risk_reason: Scaling to 0 stops the workload; scaling up consumes capacity.
cautions: --replicas=0 takes the service down.
GitOps controllers may revert manual scaling.
Scaling StatefulSets changes storage claims.
commands.explanation: Sets replicas of deployments/statefulsets.

commands.name: kubectl drain
commands.risk_reason: Evicts workloads and cordons the node; can cause outages if PDBs/replicas are insufficient.
cautions: Drain one node at a time and verify PodDisruptionBudgets.
--force deletes pods without controllers permanently.
--delete-emptydir-data destroys local emptyDir contents.
commands.explanation: Prepares a node for maintenance. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kubectl` for the full reference.

commands.name: kubectl cordon
commands.risk_reason: No new pods land on the node; capacity shrinks.
cautions: Remember to uncordon after maintenance.
commands.explanation: Prevents scheduling without evicting running pods.

commands.name: kubectl uncordon
commands.risk_reason: Resumes scheduling.
commands.explanation: Reverses cordon/drain. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kubectl` for the full reference.

commands.name: kubectl edit
commands.risk_reason: Changes take effect immediately and bypass Git review.
cautions: Production edits drift from Git; GitOps tools may revert them.
A YAML mistake can roll out a broken pod template instantly.
commands.explanation: Opens the live object in $EDITOR. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kubectl` for the full reference.

safer.why: Change via a reviewed manifest instead

commands.name: kubectl patch
commands.risk_reason: Applies a partial change immediately.
cautions: Quoting mistakes silently patch the wrong field.
Drift from Git.
commands.explanation: Strategic-merge, merge or JSON patches. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kubectl` for the full reference.

commands.name: kubectl label
commands.risk_reason: Label changes can detach pods from Services/ReplicaSets.
cautions: Changing a pod’s labels can orphan it from its controller or Service selector.
Node labels affect scheduling.
commands.explanation: Edits labels on objects. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kubectl` for the full reference.

commands.name: kubectl annotate
commands.risk_reason: Annotations can change controller behaviour.
cautions: Some annotations toggle critical behaviour (ingress, autoscaler).
commands.explanation: Edits annotations. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kubectl` for the full reference.

commands.name: kubectl taint
commands.risk_reason: Can evict pods (NoExecute) or block scheduling.
cautions: NoExecute evicts existing pods immediately.
commands.explanation: Adds/removes taints. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kubectl` for the full reference.

commands.name: kubectl port-forward
commands.risk_reason: Exposes in-cluster services to your machine.
cautions: Binding to 0.0.0.0 (--address) exposes the cluster service to your network.
Direct DB access in prod bypasses audit.
commands.explanation: Tunnel to a pod/service port. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kubectl` for the full reference.

commands.name: kubectl cp
commands.risk_reason: Overwrites files inside containers.
cautions: Requires tar in the image; copying into pods bypasses deployment pipelines.
commands.explanation: Copies between local and a pod using tar.

commands.name: kubectl create
commands.risk_reason: Creates live objects outside GitOps.
cautions: Secrets created with literals appear in shell history.
Prefer declarative manifests in Git.
commands.explanation: Creates deployments, secrets, namespaces etc.

commands.name: kubectl set image
commands.risk_reason: Triggers a rollout immediately.
cautions: Rollout replaces pods; a bad tag causes ImagePullBackOff outage.
Use pinned versions.
commands.explanation: Updates a workload’s image. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kubectl` for the full reference.

commands.name: kubectl autoscale
commands.risk_reason: Changes replica counts automatically.
cautions: A too-high max can exhaust cluster capacity and budget.
commands.explanation: Creates a HorizontalPodAutoscaler. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kubectl` for the full reference.

commands.name: kubectl auth can-i
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: Tests whether an action is allowed. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kubectl` for the full reference.

examples.cmd: kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n prod

commands.name: kubectl config
commands.risk_reason: `use-context` changes the target cluster for later commands.
cautions: Always confirm the context before destructive commands.
Kubeconfig contains credentials.
commands.explanation: View and switch contexts. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kubectl` for the full reference.

commands.name: kubectl events
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: Cluster events, useful for scheduling and pull errors.

commands.name: kubectl wait
commands.risk_reason: Read-only wait.
commands.explanation: Blocks until a condition is met. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kubectl` for the full reference.

commands.name: kubectl replace
commands.risk_reason: Overwrites the whole object; --force deletes and recreates.
cautions: --force deletes the resource first — downtime and data loss for PVCs.
commands.explanation: Replaces an object from a file. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kubectl` for the full reference.

commands.name: kubectl certificate
commands.risk_reason: Approving a CSR grants credentials.
cautions: Only approve CSRs you can attribute to a trusted requester.
commands.explanation: Approve or deny CertificateSigningRequests.

commands.name: kubeadm
commands.risk_reason: Init/reset/upgrade modify the entire control plane.
cautions: `kubeadm reset` removes cluster membership and local etcd data.
Upgrade one minor version at a time, control plane first, with etcd backup.
Expired certificates take down the API server.
commands.explanation: Cluster lifecycle tool for init, join, upgrade and certificate renewal.

flags.caution: Destroys cluster state on that node.

commands.name: etcdctl
commands.risk_reason: etcd holds all cluster state; deletes or restores can wipe the cluster.
cautions: Never write/delete keys directly in a Kubernetes etcd.
Test snapshot restores regularly.
Protect certs; etcd contains Secrets in clear unless encryption at rest is on.
commands.explanation: Reads/writes etcd keys and manages snapshots/members.

commands.name: kubectx
commands.risk_reason: Switching context changes the cluster later commands hit.
cautions: Show the context in your prompt to avoid running commands on the wrong cluster.
commands.explanation: Fast context/namespace switcher (kubens for namespaces).

commands.name: k9s
commands.risk_reason: Delete/edit shortcuts act on live objects.
cautions: Ctrl-d deletes the highlighted resource.
Use --readonly for production.
commands.explanation: Interactive cluster browser. Ctrl-d deletes, e edits, s opens a shell.

commands.name: stern
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
cautions: High-fanout tails can overload the API server.
commands.explanation: Streams logs by regex across pods. See the flags and examples below, and run `man stern` for the full reference.

commands.name: kustomize
commands.risk_reason: Rendering is read-only; applying changes the cluster.
cautions: Always review rendered output before applying.
commands.explanation: Builds overlays of YAML. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kustomize` for the full reference.

commands.name: kind
commands.risk_reason: Creates local clusters and containers.
cautions: Check kubectl context afterwards so you do not mix local and real clusters.
commands.explanation: Spins up local test clusters. See the flags and examples below, and run `man kind` for the full reference.

commands.name: minikube
commands.risk_reason: Local VM/container; changes kubectl context.
cautions: It switches your kubectl context.
commands.explanation: Runs a local cluster. See the flags and examples below, and run `man minikube` for the full reference.

commands.name: helm install
commands.risk_reason: Creates cluster resources immediately.
cautions: Verify the kube context and namespace.
Pin chart versions; review values.
commands.explanation: Installs a chart as a release. See the flags and examples below, and run `man helm` for the full reference.

commands.name: helm upgrade
commands.risk_reason: Changes live resources; --install may create new ones.
cautions: Use helm diff upgrade to see changes.
--reuse-values can carry over stale settings.
CRD changes are not upgraded by Helm.
commands.explanation: Applies a new chart version or values. See the flags and examples below, and run `man helm` for the full reference.

commands.name: helm uninstall
commands.risk_reason: Deletes every resource of the release.
cautions: Deletes Deployments/Services/Ingresses; check PVC retention.
Confirm namespace and release.
commands.explanation: Uninstalls a release; PVCs may or may not be removed.

commands.name: helm rollback
commands.risk_reason: Reverts live resources to an earlier revision.
cautions: Rolling back does not roll back databases or CRDs.
commands.explanation: Rolls back to a previous release revision.

commands.name: helm repo
commands.risk_reason: Adds third-party sources.
cautions: Only add repositories you trust; charts run with cluster privileges.
commands.explanation: Add/update chart repos. See the flags and examples below, and run `man helm` for the full reference.

commands.name: helm template
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: Outputs manifests without installing. See the flags and examples below, and run `man helm` for the full reference.

examples.cmd: helm template web ./chart -f values.yaml | kubectl diff -f -

commands.name: kubens
commands.risk_reason: Changes default namespace for your context.
cautions: A default namespace can hide that you act in production.
commands.explanation: Sets the default namespace in kubeconfig.

commands.name: istioctl
commands.risk_reason: Mesh config changes affect all traffic.
cautions: Install/uninstall and mTLS changes affect production traffic.
commands.explanation: Install, analyze and debug Istio. See the flags and examples below, and run `man istioctl` for the full reference.
